text: My name is Claire Liguori, and I'm a Senior Principal Engineer at AWS.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I mostly work on Kiro, our Agent Decoding Assistant.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But today I want to talk about some of the practices we've been seeing inside of Amazon and Amazon Teams, where we've been seeing really exciting results of productivity increases that are step function improvements since what we've been seeing with AI so far.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I've been working on agentic AI for over three years now, and I've kind of seen the evolution that's happened in our industry when it comes to coding assistance with AI.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First, we had this inline code completion helping us to write the next line, maybe the next function.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We moved on to chat, asking questions about our code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Everybody started doing vibe coding sometime last year.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But now we're starting to see kind of an early adopter phase of what we've been calling frontier development.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And completely anecdotally, based on my own experience, I've really only felt maybe 10% to 20% more productive with all of these phases that have come before.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But now inside of Amazon, we've been running pilots with different teams across the company, and we've been seeing a median of 4.5x productivity improvement and sometimes more than 10x.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So something has really changed here now that we're seeing these step function improvements in productivity.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I like to define what we've been calling frontier developers inside of Amazon by three behaviors that I've been seeing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One is hands-off coding.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Frontier developers write maybe 1% to 2% of the code that they produce.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The rest is agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The second is that they interact with their agents infrequently.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They'll aim to get their coding assistant to run for up to hours at a time without their intervention.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And third is that they minimize idle time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: These frontier developers tend to run multiple agents in parallel, churning through a backlog of tasks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The first time that I saw a Frontier developer team was the Bedrock Mantle team.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Bedrock is our model hosting service.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It hosts LLMs like Claude and GPT.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And sometime last year, we knew, or I say we, but the Bedrock team knew that they were going to need to build a new inference data plane.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But they had estimated it at 30 people over 18 months.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is a big, big service, and it was going to take time to build the new one, migrate customers over, migrate models over.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And they decided to take a step back.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They took six people, and they built it in 76 days with Curo.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this was a huge achievement.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This was the first time we'd seen anything of the kind inside of Amazon.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this was truly the Pathfinder team that proved that it was possible to get up to 20x improvement.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now they looked at commits, and I'll talk about a couple of other ways that we are measuring productivity improvements.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But there was one problem with this story, which was that, yes, it was built with six people.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It was built with some of the top engineers literally in the company, including two distinguished engineers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this was not just any team of six people.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: These were experts in distributed systems, experts at LLMs and their architecture.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this story was amazing, and it kind of spread like wildfire across Amazon, but it was also very unachievable for a lot of teams.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There were a lot of questions about, can this actually be reproduced on another team?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So another experiment that I want to talk about is an experimental sprint that was done in the Prime Video Organization.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They took a 10-day sprint and they did an experiment where they put, again, six engineers in a room and they let them go wild with Kiro.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They brought down the project delivery time estimate from what was going to be 90 weeks down to 24.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: based on all of the progress they had made in this 10-day sprint.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And they looked at their commit history and they looked at what did they used to do prior to this 10-day sprint and how many commits did they produce just in this 10 days.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so this sprint really proved that we can achieve, again, at least something close to what the Bedrock Mantle team had achieved with a different set of engineers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But again, there was a challenge with this story, which was it was six engineers in a room, but they had no on-call duties, limited meetings, very few distractions, which we all know are regular in the lives of an engineer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the senior engineer on the team had spent the previous three weeks creating very detailed, small, well-scoped tasks with detailed requirements for these six engineers to just go turn on for those two weeks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this was, again, not necessarily real life.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This was a structured sprint, a point in time that they were able to achieve this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But again, the question is, is this achievable on real teams for day-to-day work?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So Amazon Stores, which encompasses Amazon.com, all of our retail websites, as well as our physical stores, did a more structured pilot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They watched 50 teams that were totally normal, normal distribution of early career folks, mid-career senior engineers, and that worked on existing systems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Nothing Greenfield like the Mantle team got to build from the ground up.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But existing systems with existing code bases.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And they watched them for the better part of last year, and they found something super interesting.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They found that there was a big difference in the productivity gains that they saw between half of the teams and the other half.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And in this case, they used a productivity metric of deployment velocity to production.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So not just commits, how many commits are they producing, but how quickly are we getting changes out to customers?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How quickly are we able to ship things?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And they saw that for half of the teams, they achieved less than 3x increase.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And what they found that was the difference between seeing less than 3x productivity increase, these teams that saw a median of 4.5x, and in some cases more than 10, was how they use the tools.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: 90% of these teams use Kiro, among other internal tools that we have, and what they found was it wasn't about the tools, it was about the way that they worked.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The teams that achieve step function improvements intentionally changed the way that they worked, and the others simply kind of sprinkled Kiro and some of the other tools that we have on top of their existing way of working.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And for me, at least, this was the big aha moment, that why I hadn't been feeling potentially the massive gains in productivity that AI has promised.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's about changing the way that we work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So across this pilot, they went and interviewed the teams that were involved in the pilot as well as some of these other teams on the Bedrock Mantle team, on Prime Video, and they found five habits.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I use the word habits very specifically because, again, it's not about that one sprint.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's about doing this day to day.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And what they found when they interviewed with these teams was that it really was habits that they had to build day to day.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When we change our way of working,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's hard to build these habits.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It takes time to build these habits.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So let's go through each of these one by one.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Habit number one is investing in agent context.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have a lot of stuff in our head.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We tend to transfer all of that stuff in our head to other people through Slack conversations, through onboarding mentors, things like that, through code reviews, through stand-ups and sprint planning, and they had to write all of that down.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the habit that they built was every time the agent makes a mistake or does something not the way that you would have done it, what am I missing in my skills files?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What am I missing in my steering files that the agent needed?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But then, as we know, across last year, we saw leaps and bounds in models' abilities and their behaviors.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The Sonnet 3.7 in the middle of last year
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We've had a lot of quirks that we had to put a lot of do nots in our steering files.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And now we don't have to do that as much with Opus 4.5 as of last November.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then we've had six months, more than six months of improvements since then with all of the new versions of models that have come out since then.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so the question, the new habit again is, do I still need this in my steering files or is this just bloating context?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The second one is slowing down to speed up.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In almost every team that was interviewed, they reported that their productivity actually went down as they intentionally adopted a new way of working.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's counterintuitive, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You have to do intentional engineering work before you're going to see that hockey stick curve in productivity improvement because we have to do real work in our code bases first for agents to be successful there, especially in Brownfield existing code bases.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So they had to build that agent context up.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They had to improve existing tools error messages so that the model knew what was going on when it failed.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They built new tools, new MCP servers for helping that model to actually get done what it needed to get done.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A lot of teams ended up restructuring their code base so that agents could actually navigate it more easily.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I've even seen drastic changes like changing the programming language of the code base.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Often I've seen teams struggle with Python, with JavaScript because they're untyped languages.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's hard to test.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's no compiler errors.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the model kind of guesses and gives it back to you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so I've seen teams moving to TypeScript
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Rust has become very popular inside of Amazon.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The compiler gives great error messages.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You don't have to do that, but I've seen a lot of teams making those intentional changes for the productivity gains that they're able to see.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The third one is feeding agents, not babysitting agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And for me, this was one of those aha moments of why we're seeing this step function improvement in productivity.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you are vibe coding, if you are having a back and forth conversation with your agent all day long, of course, you're not going to see
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: 4 to 5x productivity improvements because you are in the loop the entire time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You're probably sitting there for 30 seconds to a minute waiting for it to generate code and come back to you with the code to review.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you're sitting there waiting for it, then you can't go off and do other stuff.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's really difficult to run agents in parallel.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's very difficult to clone yourself into multiple agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so if your conversations look a bit like this on the left, then you're babysitting that agent, as opposed to the right side where you're feeding it what it needs to do and how it can self-validate.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that's really the key so that agents can self-correct and only come back to you when it meets a certain quality bar, when it actually runs and compiles and passes tests, when it's testable, when it actually has high coverage.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And of course, the next level is put all of this content into your steering file so it does it every time without you having to prompt it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The fourth habit is to make intent explicit.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: At Amazon, we practice a lot of spectrum and development.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We've built that into the Kiro product.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so it's very natural for Amazon engineers to adopt it in Kiro.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What I've typically seen with vibe coding as opposed to frontier engineering is giving a very high level prompt, letting the agent generate a ton of code,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then having a back and forth conversation saying, oh, that's not really what I meant.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You haven't exactly gotten the requirements right.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: No, I didn't actually want to build it that way.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Here's a technical design.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it is less, I find, less productive to iterate with the agent on code when the intent itself was incorrect.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So often we'll see Amazon engineers go through this process for ambiguous, complex features of writing the specification.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And in Curo, of course, you don't have to write this whole specification.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can have the model generate it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But it's a lot easier to iterate with the model in kind of a back and forth conversation about a document than it is about code changes that are spread across a code base.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The fifth one is shift testing left.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One of the keys here is to give the agent that fast feedback loop because that's what lets it go off for hours at a time and self-correct.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The agent is going to make mistakes and that's fine, but if you give it the right signals, it can self-correct and it can spend a while doing that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I've seen teams adding linters, adding unit tests, integration tests, performance tests, security tests.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: These are all things we all know we should have been doing all along.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is good engineering hygiene and practices.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But now the ROI is, I think, finally high enough for us to actually invest in it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One thing that I've been seeing a lot of teams do is mock-out services.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Often with integration tests, we would test kind of end-to-end an entire system, including live services.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But we've been investing a lot in mock services that run entirely locally with deterministic responses.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Because it lets the agent do everything locally.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Doing everything on your laptop without having to spin up a bunch of other services and connect to cloud services makes everything a lot faster.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Because the more that your agent can get fast feedback means the more loops that it can do and the more productive your own agent can be.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So across all of these, these are some of the habits we've seen.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But of course, I would be remiss if I would tell you if you adopt all of these habits, you will achieve nirvana.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You will be the most productive engineering organization the world has ever seen.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Things are still hard.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We are still very much in an early adopter phase, and teams are still figuring it out.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So one thing that we've been seeing across our teams just organizationally is the risk of burnout.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I did not coin this term.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I forget who did at what conference, but FOMAT is real.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We've been seeing engineers staying up late, late at night, trying to get that perfect prompt that's going to make their agent run for hours overnight so that they wake up in the morning with a code change ready.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The cognitive load increases as you run these multiple agents in parallel.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You're constantly shifting between terminal tabs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then we do see that reviewing AI output is often harder for some than actually writing it, especially early in career.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Senior engineers have already spent a large portion of their career reviewing others' code, but early career engineers don't have that muscle yet.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so reviewing it can feel like a lot more cognitive load than they're used to in actually writing it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The other one is organizational change.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So it's already hard to change the way we work as engineers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The way that we spend our entire day completely changes when we're Frontier engineers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But also organizations have to change to enable Frontier engineering teams.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One that I've seen very commonly is accepting slowing down to speed up.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I've been guilty of this myself.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: My fellow leaders have been guilty of this, of saying, well, you have the AI tools now and the models are so amazing now.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Why are you not going faster?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that's because you have to take those two months to invest in your code base, to figure out the best practices for your team, to make hard habit changes on your team.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And if you're constantly expecting...
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Shipping features every month because now we have these amazing models and we're seeing all of these companies on X saying how they're shipping 20 PRs a day.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have to slow down to speed up.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The second one is actually going too broad in the organization too fast.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I think that if we had expected all teams in massive organizations to be frontier teams immediately, we would not have had the learnings that we had from the Pathfinder, from the Sprint experiment, from the pilot,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: teams within Amazon.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And now the challenge for us is how do we scale it out?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that's what 2026 is about for Amazon is how do we scale this out to more and more teams to the next
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: 2,000 teams instead of 50 teams.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so I think that when you roll it out too quickly, you have a lot of teams who don't know what they're doing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You haven't had time to find the best practices for your own organizations, the context that your organization needs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the last one is that you're going to find new bottlenecks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Previously, writing code manually was the bottleneck.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I find that within Amazon, we've found the speed of decision-making becomes a new bottleneck.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The more that you spend reviewing the decision to actually build a new product, the slower it is to build the product now because the code only takes one to two months to write.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: All of the review processes associated with the launch of a product become the bottleneck.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When it used to take 9 to 12 months to build a new product, it didn't matter so much in the overall wash of things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If it took two months to make the decision to build the product and then two months to approve the launch.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But now those are the bottlenecks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Those are the long pole.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so you find all of these things that slow you down.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Often I find that frontier engineering teams spend more time making decisions than they do writing code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so the more that you can make fast decisions, especially ones that are easy to be reversed, the better.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So my one big takeaway for everyone here is that frontier engineering is about intentionally changing the way that you work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that is difficult.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That takes time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It is forming new habits and a new way of working.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that goes across any engineering team as well as your organization.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I encourage you to think about how you're interacting with AI tools and how that can change to free yourself up from being in the loop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Thanks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'll hang out a little bit if anyone has questions in the back.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But thanks for the time today.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Thank you.
